summary: Describes the ARIA encryption algorithm, a block cipher that works on 128-bit blocks and supports 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys. It consists of a key scheduling part and a data randomizing part. This is an informational description, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes ARIA, a block cipher made in Korea. It gives the exact steps for turning a key into round keys and for encrypting a block, so that an implementer can reproduce the same results as anyone else.

questions: how many rounds does aria use
what key sizes does aria support
how does the aria key schedule work
subtitle: A 128-bit block cipher from Korea, described in enough detail to implement.

tldr.problem: A cipher has to be described precisely enough that two independent implementations produce the same results, which means the specification cannot leave the round structure or the lookup tables to the reader.
tldr.mechanism: The document gives the key schedule, the round functions, the four substitution boxes, the diffusion layer, and the encryption and decryption processes for all three key sizes, together with test vectors.
tldr.outcome: ARIA encrypts 128-bit blocks with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys in 12, 14 or 16 rounds, and the document reports that its security was analysed by a research group that found no flaw.

today: RFC 5794 is an Informational Independent Submission published in March 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes an algorithm rather than defining a standard, and the text records that ARIA was established as a Korean standard block cipher in 2004 and was included in PKCS #11 in 2007.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
ARIA is a general-purpose block cipher algorithm developed by Korean cryptographers in 2003. It is an iterated block cipher with 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys, and it encrypts 128-bit blocks in 12, 14 and 16 rounds respectively, depending on the key size. It is secure and suitable for most software and hardware implementations on 32-bit and 8-bit processors. It was established as a Korean standard block cipher algorithm in 2004 and has been widely used in Korea, especially for government-to-public services, and it was included in PKCS #11 in 2007.

The algorithm consists of two parts. The key scheduling part turns the master key into the round keys used by each round, and the data randomizing part performs the encryption and decryption itself. The notation used in the document is simple: a caret for bitwise exclusive or, triple angle brackets for left and right circular rotation, double bars for concatenation of bit strings, and the 0x prefix for hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: ARIA always works on a block of 128 bits at a time. The key length changes how many rounds the encryption goes through, so a longer key means more rounds and more work.

sections.title: The Key Scheduling Part
sections.content:
Given a master key K of 128, 192 or 256 bits, two 128-bit values KL and KR are defined so that KL concatenated with KR equals the key padded with zeros, where the number of zeros is 128, 64 or 0 depending on the key size. In other words, KL is the leftmost 128 bits of K and KR holds the remaining bits, if any, right-padded with zeros to 128 bits.

Four 128-bit values W0, W1, W2 and W3 are then defined as the intermediate round values appearing in the encryption of KL concatenated with KR by a 3-round, 256-bit Feistel cipher: W0 is KL, W1 is the odd round function applied to W0 and CK1, exclusive or KR, W2 is the even round function applied to W1 and CK2, exclusive or W0, and W3 is the odd round function applied to W2 and CK3, exclusive or W1.

The constants CK1, CK2 and CK3 are 128-bit values chosen from three published constants, C1, C2 and C3, which are obtained from the first 384 bits of the fractional part of one over pi. Which constant is used in which position depends on the key size: with a 128-bit key the three are C1, C2 and C3 in order; with a 192-bit key they are C2, C3 and C1; with a 256-bit key they are C3, C1 and C2.

The encryption round keys ek1 to ek17 are computed from W0 to W3 by a fixed list of combinations of exclusive or and rotation: the first four use a right rotation by 19 bits, the next four a right rotation by 31 bits, the next four a left rotation by 61 bits, the next four a left rotation by 31 bits, and the last one a left rotation by 19 bits.

The number of rounds depends on the size of the master key: 12 rounds for a 128-bit key, 14 for 192 bits and 16 for 256 bits. Because of an extra key addition layer in the last round, these need 13, 15 and 17 round keys respectively. Decryption round keys are derived from the encryption round keys: the first decryption key is the last encryption key, the intermediate decryption keys are the encryption keys in reverse order with the diffusion layer applied, and the last decryption key is the first encryption key.
sections.plainLanguage: The key schedule splits the master key in half, runs it through three rounds of a Feistel cipher to produce four intermediate values, and combines those values with rotations to produce one round key per round. Longer keys select a different order for the three constants.

sections.title: The Data Randomizing Part
sections.content:
The data randomizing part consists of the encryption and decryption processes, and uses the round functions, the diffusion layer and the two substitution layers. For a 128-bit plain text and a 128-bit master key, with the thirteen round keys defined by the key schedule, the cipher text is computed as twelve rounds alternating the odd and even round functions, starting with the odd one, and then a final round that exclusive-ors the result of the eleventh round with round key twelve, passes it through the second substitution layer, and exclusive-ors the result with round key thirteen.

The 192-bit key case is the same with fifteen round keys and fourteen rounds, ending with an exclusive-or of the thirteenth round with round key fourteen, the second substitution layer, and an exclusive-or with round key fifteen. The 256-bit key case uses seventeen round keys and sixteen rounds, ending with the fifteenth round exclusive-ored with round key sixteen, the second substitution layer, and an exclusive-or with round key seventeen.

Decryption is the same process with the encryption round keys replaced by the decryption round keys, so the thirteen round keys of the 12-round algorithm are replaced by the thirteen decryption round keys in the same order.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption is a fixed number of rounds, alternating two slightly different round functions and adding a different round key each time. The last round is different: it adds a key before and after the substitution step. Decryption runs the same steps with the round keys in reverse order.

sections.title: The Components of ARIA
sections.content:
There are two round functions. The odd round function takes a pair of 128-bit strings, the data and the round key, and outputs the diffusion layer applied to the first substitution layer of the data exclusive-ored with the round key. The even round function takes the same inputs and outputs the diffusion layer applied to the second substitution layer of the data exclusive-ored with the round key.

The two substitution layers alternate between rounds, with the first used in the odd rounds and the second in the even rounds. Each takes a 16-byte string and produces a 16-byte string by replacing each byte with the output of one of four substitution boxes: the first layer applies the boxes in the order SB1, SB2, SB3, SB4 and repeats that order four times across the sixteen bytes, while the second layer applies SB3, SB4, SB1, SB2 and repeats that order. Each box takes an 8-bit input and produces an 8-bit output, and the tables are given in full in the document, with the example that SB1 of 0x23 is 0x26 and SB4 of 0xef is 0xd3. The third and fourth boxes are the inverse functions of the first and second, so the second substitution layer is the inverse of the first.

The diffusion layer takes a 16-byte string and produces a 16-byte string by exclusive-oring groups of seven of the input bytes for each output byte, following a fixed table of equations. One property the document notes is that the diffusion layer is an involution: applying it twice to any input gives the original input back.
sections.plainLanguage: Each round mixes the data in two steps. The substitution step replaces every byte with a value looked up in one of four tables, and the diffusion step combines bytes with each other so that a change to one byte spreads across the block.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that ARIA is designed to be resistant to all known attacks on block ciphers. Its security was analysed by the COSIC group of K.U. Leuven in Belgium, and no security flaw has been found.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say the cipher was analysed by an outside research group, which found no flaw in it. The document offers no analysis of its own.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS A ROUND IS BUILT FROM

items.title: Odd round function
items.text: Adds the round key, then the first substitution layer, then the diffusion layer.

items.title: Even round function
items.text: Adds the round key, then the second substitution layer, then the diffusion layer.

items.title: Substitution layers
items.text: Replace each of the sixteen bytes through one of four lookup tables, in one of two alternating orders.

items.title: Diffusion layer
items.text: Exclusive-ors groups of seven input bytes to make each output byte; applying it twice returns the input.
